reasons: The title says 'verified' but the file says the dates are unverified upload claims.
Citation markers are left in the text.
Only 3 of 7 sections were supplied for review.

terms.meaning: A report a public company files with the US Securities and Exchange Commission.
The yearly and quarterly financial reports public companies file with the SEC.
Project spending recorded as part of the asset's value on the balance sheet, not as a yearly expense.
Engineering, procurement and construction contractor who builds the project.
Checking a claim against its original source.

sections.name: File setup (part 1)
sections.title: Report header and qualifying rule
sections.what: Opens with a warning that the report's access dates are claims in the upload, then sets the strict rule that a project counts only when a source says more than US$1 billion was spent. It lists the nine qualifying projects with cited amounts and a timeline of milestones.
sections.why: The report says it uses a strict standard on purpose, so only explicitly stated spending counts.
sections.watch_out: Amounts are shown in mixed currencies and the access dates are unverified, so do not treat the list as checked.

sections.name: File setup (part 2)
sections.title: Budget versus actual cost comparison
sections.what: Compares each project's original and revised budgets with its reported spend, and states what each figure includes or leaves out. The report declines to calculate overruns. The section also begins the project records, starting with CityCenter.
sections.why: Likely reason: budgets and spend use different scope definitions, so the report keeps them side by side rather than merging them.
sections.watch_out: Budgets include different items such as land, interest and pre-opening costs, so direct comparison can mislead. A dash in a table means not reported, not zero.

sections.name: File setup (part 3)
sections.title: Marina Bay Sands project records
sections.what: Gives field-by-field records for the original Marina Bay Sands development and its Expansion Project. Each entry lists cost, opening or construction dates, financing and a cited filing. Fields the sources did not state are marked with a dash.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: The expansion's estimate and its incurred amount are at different dates and scopes, so do not subtract one from the other without checking the sources.

sections.name: File setup (part 4)
sections.title: Wynn Palace and Encore Boston Harbor records
sections.what: Two fact tables on large casino resorts, one in Macau and one in Massachusetts. Each row gives a figure such as a budget, an amount spent or an opening date, with a source note beside it. Below each table is a numbered source record with a web address and a quoted sentence from the filing.
sections.why: Likely reason: the research is written so that each figure can be traced to a specific document and date.
sections.watch_out: Strings such as citeturn0search4 are leftover search-tool markers, not working links, so they appear as plain text and should be removed or ignored.

sections.name: File setup (part 5)
sections.title: Studio City, Sphere and Huntsville scope warning
sections.what: The Studio City table lists a Macau resort's site size, budget and October 2015 opening. The Sphere table lists a Las Vegas venue whose cost estimates rose over time, with about $2.25bn paid through August 2023. The Huntsville part warns that the city and company figures measure different things.
sections.why: Likely reason: the Sphere entries record each cost estimate with its date, because the estimates changed over time.
sections.watch_out: The Huntsville warning says the $3bn and $1bn figures cover different scopes, so a reader must not treat either one as the full project total.

sections.name: File setup (part 6)
sections.title: Huntsville, Baha Mar and excluded-list setup
sections.what: Holds the Huntsville data center table and its sources, the Baha Mar table with a weaker source note, and the start of a list of projects left out of the strict set. The Baha Mar $3.5bn figure comes through a newspaper that attributes it to the Central Bank, and the original bank document was not retrieved.
sections.why: Likely reason: the research set was kept strict, so projects without a clear actual-spend figure were moved to a separate list instead of being counted.
sections.watch_out: The Baha Mar figure rests on a secondhand report, so its evidence is weaker than the SEC filings used for other projects.

sections.name: File setup (part 7)
sections.title: Excluded projects and the rule behind them
sections.what: A table of large projects that were not counted in the strict list, with the reason for each. It explains that development value, future commitments and summed yearly spending are not the same as money actually spent. The closing text says each admitted figure is kept with its source, date and scope, and is not converted, added up or estimated.
sections.why: Likely reason: the author wanted the list to be traceable and to keep budget, spending and investment value separate.
sections.watch_out: Some excluded projects, such as MGM Cotai, may well pass the $1bn threshold, so their exclusion is a rule-based choice and not evidence that they are small.

summary: A research report, not application code, listing large real-estate and entertainment projects where public sources say actual spending topped US$1 billion.
purpose: Gives a checked list of big projects with cited sources, budgets and spending figures.
why: Likely reason: the report explains it applies a deliberately strict rule, so a project counts only when a source states spending above US$1 billion. The original request is not in the file.
how: 1. Sets the rule for qualifying a project. 2. Lists nine qualifying projects with cited amounts. 3. Compares original budgets with reported spend. 4. Gives status and schedule tables. 5. Gives field-by-field records and source entries for each project.
inputs: An uploaded research report, public sources such as SEC filings, company releases and government documents, and a field schema from the user.
outputs: A single web page with a summary, tables, a timeline and source records.
risks: Amounts are in mixed currencies and dates. The file itself says its access dates are claims from the upload and not verified. Citation markers from the research tool remain in the text.
debug: Check each cited source and its date. Search the file for 'citeturn' to find leftover citation markers. Compare the stated figures with the source documents before relying on them.
